This one is above your threshold, 6 files. Want to predict while it works? Say skip to pass.

Two questions, then I will leave you alone until it is done. I will not tell you whether you are right yet.

Easy call: server/routes/auth.js, server/controllers/authController.js, server/models/User.js, server/lib/mailer.js, client/src/routes.jsx, and client/src/pages/Login.jsx since that's where the forgot-password link will live.
You said pages are auto-registered by filename, so a new page needs no routing change, yet you listed routes.jsx. What would actually need to change there, if anything?

Right, if pages auto-register by filename then routes.jsx shouldn't need touching for the new pages themselves, I was thinking of it needing an update for the new path strings like /forgot-password and /reset-password/:token, but if the router just scans the pages folder those get picked up too. I'll stick with routes.jsx staying in my six for now since token params usually need explicit path definitions.

Noted, routes.jsx stays on your list with that reasoning. Now set files aside: walk me through what happens step by step, from the moment the user clicks "forgot password" to the moment they are logged in with a new password.
Agent needs you. I will wait.
Back. Nothing else from me until it is done.

User clicks "forgot password" on the login page, which takes them to a ForgotPassword page where they type their email and submit. The client calls an API like requestPasswordReset, the server looks up the user, generates a reset token, and saves it on the User model with an expiry. The server emails a link containing that token via mailer.js. User clicks the link, lands on ResetPassword page which reads the token from the URL, user types a new password, and the client hashes the password before sending it along with the token to the server. Server verifies the token and expiry, updates the user's password in the database, and then logs the user in automatically by issuing a new session or JWT, redirecting them to Notes.

Got it, that's a clear walkthrough. One thing to sit with: you said the client hashes the password before sending it, but crypto.js lives under server/lib. Don't answer now, just turn that over while the agent finishes.

You named one file, routes.jsx, and it wasn't actually changed. Of the six files that were planned and did change, you named zero.

Here's what was in the plan that you didn't mention: ForgotPassword.jsx and ResetPassword.jsx are new pages, one takes an email and calls a reset request, the other reads a token from the URL and posts a new password. client/src/api/auth.js adds the two functions that call those endpoints. server/routes/auth.js declares the two new POST routes. server/controllers/authController.js does the real work, generates a token, hashes it, stores it with a one hour expiry, and on reset checks the hash and expiry before updating the password. server/models/User.js just gets two new fields to hold that hash and expiry. I don't have the actual diff lines in front of me for these, so I won't invent code, but that's the shape of it.

One more thing: server/middleware/rateLimit.js was added and it wasn't in the plan at all, you couldn't have predicted it. I'll come back to what it does in a moment.

Given all that, has anything changed in how you'd describe the end to end flow from before?

Yeah, the password hashing happens server-side in authController, not on the client, crypto.js was my tell and I misread it since it's in server/lib. The rest of the flow holds up fine though: email link with token, token verified against the stored hash and expiry, password updated, and I'd guess the login-after-reset step either isn't automatic and just redirects to the login page, or I'm still overconfident there too.

Your steps match. Two things you didn't say: the pages don't call the server directly, they go through requestReset and submitReset in client/src/api/auth.js, which is this repo's convention for where a request lives.

```
await requestReset(email);
```
```
await submitReset(token, password);
```

And the token itself is made on the server, inside authController, not in the browser, because a token the client could generate is one anyone could forge.

Now server/middleware/rateLimit.js, the one that was not in the plan. Before I explain it - do you know what Express middleware is?

Yeah, Express middleware is a function that sits in the request pipeline and runs before the route handler, it gets access to req, res, and next, and can modify the request, short-circuit it with a response, or pass control along. Given it's called rateLimit.js, I'd guess it's there to throttle repeated calls to the forgot-password endpoint so someone can't hammer it to spam emails or brute-force tokens.

That matches what it does. Concretely, it counts timestamps per IP and once there have been six hits to /auth/forgot inside a fifteen minute window, the seventh gets a 429 instead of reaching your controller.

```
if (recent.length >= 6) return res.status(429).json({ error: 'Too many requests' });
```

This file was not part of the plan you gave the agent, it added it on its own. Whether you keep it is your call, not mine, and I won't touch the code either way.

Last one. To change how long a reset link stays valid, from one hour to six, which file do you edit?
That's the expiry value set in server/controllers/authController.js, where the token hash and expiry get stored, so you'd change the one hour constant there.

Correct. The line is in forgot(), where user.resetTokenExpiry gets set to Date.now() + 60 * 60 * 1000.
